posts.title: What happens at a February open day
posts.excerpt: The open day for the February 2027 intake is on Saturday 16 January, with a ward tour, a bandage to try and time with the tutors.
posts.content:
The open day for the February 2027 intake is on Saturday 16 January 2027, from 10:00 to 13:00. It is the easiest way to see the ward before you apply, and you do not need to book.

The morning, in order

You arrive at 10:00 for tea and a short welcome in the lecture room. At 10:30 groups of six walk the ward with a tutor and a student: the kennels, the prep room, the theatre and the imaging room. At 11:15 you go to the skills room, where a tutor shows you a bandage on a soft model leg and you try one yourself.

At 12:00 Pieter de Wit and Aisha Rahman talk about how to apply, what the course costs and how placements are matched. The last 45 minutes are for questions with tutors and current students. The ward closes to visitors at 13:00; the admissions office stays open until 17:00.

If you cannot come on the Saturday, ward visits run on Wednesdays at 15:30 for up to six visitors. Wear closed shoes.

posts.title: How placement blocks are matched to clinics
posts.excerpt: Placement is 40 weeks in 22 partner clinics. Here is how Aisha Rahman matches each student to a block.
posts.content:
Every diploma student spends 40 weeks on placement, spread across the two years, in one of our 22 partner clinics and animal hospitals. Each clinic takes one or two students in a block, so a student is never lost in a crowd.

Who decides

Aisha Rahman, our placements coordinator, makes the match. She looks at three things: how far the student can travel, what interests them, and which skills they still need to practise. A student who has done little theatre work, for instance, is likely to be placed in a clinic with a busy theatre.

Once a block is confirmed, the student is told the name of the clinic. Aisha visits during the block and meets the student and the clinic supervisor afterwards. Students keep a log, which comes back to college, where their tutor uses it to plan the next stretch of practice.

A placement is part of the course, not a job offer. If your clinic would like to host students, write to the admissions office.

posts.title: Low-stress handling: the first thing we teach
posts.excerpt: Before you meet a patient you learn to approach, hold and move an animal calmly. Here is why it comes first.
posts.content:
In the first week of the diploma you do not touch a patient. You learn, in the skills room, how to approach a dog or a cat so that it stays calm, and how to hold it so that it feels secure.

Why it comes first

A calm animal is easier to examine, easier to treat and faster to recover. A frightened animal is harder for everyone, and it is also more likely to hurt itself or the student. Everything we teach later, from taking a pulse to positioning for an X-ray, rests on the first week.

Owen Mbeki leads the sessions. He shows how to read an animal's body language, how to wrap a cat gently in a towel, and how to ask a patient to stand without pushing it. You practise on models first and then, once your tutor is sure of your hands, on a calm patient with a tutor beside you.

The same habits are in every handling session afterwards: slow movements, quiet voices, and a pause to check how the animal is. They are the habits partner clinics tell us they notice first.
